title: Book 5 — Terpsichore, Chapter 92
paragraphs: So they spoke; but the majority of the allies did not approve of their words. The rest kept silent, but the Corinthian Socles spoke as follows: “Surely now the heavens shall be beneath the earth, and the earth raised up high above the heavens; men shall have their dwelling in the sea, and fishes that habitation which men had before—seeing that you, Lacedaemonians, are doing away with free governments and are preparing to bring tyranny back into our cities, than which there is nothing more unjust or more murderous among men. For if this really seems good to you—that cities should be ruled by tyrants—then you yourselves first set up a tyrant in your own state, and then try to establish them for others. As it is, you are acting unfairly toward your allies, seeing that you have had no experience of tyrants yourselves and take the greatest care at Sparta that such a thing may never come to pass. Yet had you had experience of it, as we have had, you would be able to contribute juster opinions about it than you do now. For the established order of the Corinthian state was this: the government was an oligarchy, and the oligarchs, who were called the Bacchiadae, controlled the state and intermarried among themselves. One of these men, named Amphion, had a daughter born to him who was lame, and her name was Labda. Since none of the Bacchiadae was willing to marry her, she was taken to wife by Aëtion son of Echecrates, of the deme of Petra, but by descent a Lapith and of the race of Caeneus. Neither from her nor from any other wife were children born to him, so he set out to Delphi to inquire about offspring; and as he entered, the priestess addressed him immediately with these lines:
“‘Much to be honored are you, yet no one honors you. Labda conceives, and a rolling boulder will she bear, which shall fall down upon the heads of kings, and bring chastisement to Corinth.’

This answer given to Aëtion was somehow reported to the Bacchiadae, to whom a previous oracle delivered at Corinth had not been intelligible—an oracle that referred to the same thing as Aëtion's and ran thus:

“‘An eagle conceives in the rocks, and shall bear a ravening lion, strong and fierce to devour, who shall loosen the knees of many. Ponder this well in your minds, I bid you, Corinthians, whose dwelling lies about fair Peirene's spring and in craggy Corinth.’

This oracle, I say, having come before to the Bacchiadae, was obscure; but when afterwards they heard the one given to Aëtion, at once they understood the earlier one also, that it was in accord with Aëtion's; and understanding this second one as well, they kept quiet, intending to destroy the offspring that would be born to Aëtion. As soon, then, as his wife had borne the child, they sent ten of their own number to the deme where Aëtion lived, to kill the child. When these men had come to Petra and passed into the courtyard of Aëtion's house, they asked for the child; and Labda, knowing nothing of the purpose for which they had come and supposing them to be asking for the child out of friendly feeling for its father, brought it and placed it in the hands of one of them. They had, it seems, resolved along the way that whichever of them first received the child should dash it on the ground. However, when Labda brought and gave it, it happened by divine providence that the child smiled at the man who received it; and when he noticed this, a feeling of compassion prevented him from killing it, and in this compassion he handed it to the next man, and he to the third. Thus it passed through the hands of all ten, each handing it on, since none of them could bring himself to destroy its life. So they gave the child back to its mother and went out; and standing by the doors, they abused and reproached one another, laying blame especially on the one who had first received the child, because he had not done what had been decided. At last, after some time, they resolved to go in again and all take a share in the murder. But from the offspring of Aëtion it was fated that evils should spring up for Corinth. For Labda had been listening to all this as she stood close by the door; and fearing that they might change their minds and take the child a second time and kill it, she took it and hid it in the place that seemed to her least likely to be discovered—a corn-chest—knowing that if they returned and began to search, they were likely to examine everything. And this is just what happened. When they had come, and their search had failed to find it, they thought it best to return and say to those who had sent them that they had done everything they had been charged with. So they went away and said this; and afterwards the son of Aëtion grew up, and because he had escaped this danger, he was given the surname Cypselus, derived from the corn-chest (cypsele). When Cypselus had come to manhood and was seeking a divination, a two-edged answer was given to him at Delphi; trusting in it, he made an attempt upon Corinth and took possession of it. The answer was this:
“‘Happy indeed is the lot of this man who enters my dwelling, offspring of Aëtion; he shall rule in famous Corinth—Cypselus, he and his sons, but his children's children no longer.’

Such was the oracle. And Cypselus, when he became tyrant, was a man of this character: many of the Corinthians he drove into exile, many he deprived of their wealth, and very many more of their lives. And when he had reigned thirty years and brought his life to a prosperous end, his son Periander became his successor in the tyranny. Now Periander at first was milder than his father; but after he had corresponded through messengers with Thrasybulus, tyrant of Miletus, he became far more murderous even than Cypselus. For he sent a messenger to Thrasybulus to ask what arrangement of affairs was safest for him to make in order to govern his state best. Thrasybulus led the messenger who had come from Periander out of the city and went into a field of growing corn; as he passed through the crop, asking and asking again about the reason for his coming from Corinth, he kept cutting off the heads of any ears of corn he saw standing higher than the rest, and as he cut them off he threw them away, until he had destroyed in this way the finest and richest part of the crop. So having passed through the place and suggested not a single word of counsel, he dismissed the messenger. When the messenger returned to Corinth, Periander was eager to hear the counsel he had been given; but the messenger said that Thrasybulus had given him no counsel at all, and added that he marveled at Periander for sending him to such a man, who was out of his senses and a destroyer of his own goods—relating at the same time what he had seen Thrasybulus do. So Periander, understanding what had been done and perceiving that Thrasybulus was counseling him to put to death the most eminent men among his subjects, from that moment began to display every kind of evil treatment toward the citizens of the state. Whatever Cypselus had left undone in killing and banishing, Periander completed. In a single day he stripped all the wives of the Corinthians of their clothing on account of his own wife Melissa. For he had sent messengers to the Thesprotians on the river Acheron to consult the oracle of the dead about a deposit left with him by a guest-friend; and Melissa appeared and said that she would not tell in what place the deposit was laid, for she was cold and had no clothes, since those he had buried with her were of no use to her, not having been burned. As evidence that she was speaking the truth, she said, he should recall that he had put his loaves into a cold oven. When the report of this was brought back to Periander, the token convinced him, because he had had intercourse with Melissa after she was dead; and immediately upon receiving the message, he proclaimed that all the wives of the Corinthians should come out to the temple of Hera. They came as to a festival, in their finest adornment; and he, having stationed the spearmen of his guard in ambush, stripped them all alike—free women and their attendants—and gathering all their clothes together in a pit, he set them on fire, praying at the same time to Melissa. After he had done this and sent a second time, the apparition of Melissa told him the place where he had laid the deposit entrusted to him by his guest-friend.

“Such a thing, Lacedaemonians, you must know, is tyranny, and such are its deeds; and we Corinthians marveled greatly at first when we saw that you were sending for Hippias, and now we marvel still more because you say these things. And we adjure you, calling upon the gods of Hellas, not to establish tyrannies in the cities. If, however, you will not desist from your purpose but try to restore Hippias contrary to what is just, know that the Corinthians at least do not give their consent to what you are doing.”
